claim: NBI-921352 (formerly XEN901) is a novel sodium channel inhibitor designed to specifically target NaV1.6 channels.
source: NBI-921352 (formerly XEN901) is a novel sodium channel inhibitor designed to specifically target NaV1.6 channels.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a description of the compound.

claim: Gain-of-function mutations in SCN8A lead to excess NaV1.6 sodium current.
source: Such a molecule provides a precision-medicine approach to target SCN8A-related epilepsy syndromes (SCN8A-RES), where gain-of-function (GoF) mutations lead to excess NaV1.6 sodium current, or other indications where NaV1.6 mediated hyper-excitability contributes to disease (Gardella and Møller, 2019; Johannesen et al., 2019; Veeramah et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Gardella and Møller, 2019; Johannesen et al., 2019; Veeramah et al., 2012).

claim: NBI-921352 is a potent inhibitor of NaV1.6 with an IC50 of 0.051 µM.
source: NBI-921352 is a potent inhibitor of NaV1.6 (IC500.051 µM), with exquisite selectivity over other sodium channel isoforms (selectivity ratios of 756 X for NaV1.1, 134 X for NaV1.2, 276 X for NaV1.7, and >583 Xfor NaV1.3, NaV1.4, and NaV1.5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from automated patch-clamp experiments as described in the results section and shown in Figure 1 and Table 1.

claim: NBI-921352 has a selectivity ratio of 756-fold for NaV1.6 over NaV1.1.
source: NBI-921352 is a potent inhibitor of NaV1.6 (IC500.051 µM), with exquisite selectivity over other sodium channel isoforms (selectivity ratios of 756 X for NaV1.1, 134 X for NaV1.2, 276 X for NaV1.7, and >583 Xfor NaV1.3, NaV1.4, and NaV1.5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from automated patch-clamp experiments comparing IC50 values across isoforms.

claim: NBI-921352 has a selectivity ratio of 134-fold for NaV1.6 over NaV1.2.
source: NBI-921352 is a potent inhibitor of NaV1.6 (IC500.051 µM), with exquisite selectivity over other sodium channel isoforms (selectivity ratios of 756 X for NaV1.1, 134 X for NaV1.2, 276 X for NaV1.7, and >583 Xfor NaV1.3, NaV1.4, and NaV1.5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from automated patch-clamp experiments comparing IC50 values across isoforms.

claim: NBI-921352 has a selectivity ratio of 276-fold for NaV1.6 over NaV1.7.
source: NBI-921352 is a potent inhibitor of NaV1.6 (IC500.051 µM), with exquisite selectivity over other sodium channel isoforms (selectivity ratios of 756 X for NaV1.1, 134 X for NaV1.2, 276 X for NaV1.7, and >583 Xfor NaV1.3, NaV1.4, and NaV1.5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from automated patch-clamp experiments comparing IC50 values across isoforms.

claim: NBI-921352 has a selectivity ratio of greater than 583-fold for NaV1.6 over NaV1.3, NaV1.4, and NaV1.5.
source: NBI-921352 is a potent inhibitor of NaV1.6 (IC500.051 µM), with exquisite selectivity over other sodium channel isoforms (selectivity ratios of 756 X for NaV1.1, 134 X for NaV1.2, 276 X for NaV1.7, and >583 Xfor NaV1.3, NaV1.4, and NaV1.5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from automated patch-clamp experiments comparing IC50 values across isoforms.

claim: NBI-921352 is a state-dependent inhibitor that preferentially inhibits inactivated channels.
source: NBI-921352is a state-dependent inhibitor, preferentially inhibiting inactivatedchannels.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from voltage-clamp protocols showing differential potency at different holding potentials (Figure 3).

claim: NBI-921352 stabilizes inactivation and inhibits NaV1.6 currents, including resurgent and persistent NaV1.6 currents, while sparing closed/rested channels.
source: The state dependence leads to potent stabilization of inactivation, inhibiting NaV1.6 currents, including resurgent and persistent NaV1.6 currents, while sparing the closed/rested channels.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from voltage-clamp protocols measuring different current types (Figure 3).

claim: NBI-921352 robustly inhibits action-potential firing in glutamatergic excitatory pyramidal neurons.
source: The isoform-selective profile of NBI-921352 led to a robust inhibition of action-potential firing in glutamatergic excitatory pyramidal neurons, while sparing fast-spiking inhibitory interneurons, where NaV1.1 predominates.
evidence: This claim is supported by current-clamp electrophysiology data from brain slice experiments (Figure 4).

claim: NBI-921352 spares fast-spiking inhibitory interneurons where NaV1.1 predominates.
source: The isoform-selective profile of NBI-921352 led to a robust inhibition of action-potential firing in glutamatergic excitatory pyramidal neurons, while sparing fast-spiking inhibitory interneurons, where NaV1.1 predominates.
evidence: This claim is supported by current-clamp electrophysiology data from brain slice experiments (Figure 4).

claim: Oral administration of NBI-921352 prevented electrically induced seizures in a Scn8a GoF mouse.
source: Oral administration of NBI-921352 prevented electrically induced seizures in a Scn8a GoF mouse,as well as in wild-type mouse and ratseizure models.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo seizure assay data (Figure 5).

claim: Oral administration of NBI-921352 prevented electrically induced seizures in wild-type mouse seizure models.
source: Oral administration of NBI-921352 prevented electrically induced seizures in a Scn8a GoF mouse,as well as in wild-type mouse and ratseizure models.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo seizure assay data (Figure 5).

claim: Oral administration of NBI-921352 prevented electrically induced seizures in wild-type rat seizure models.
source: Oral administration of NBI-921352 prevented electrically induced seizures in a Scn8a GoF mouse,as well as in wild-type mouse and ratseizure models.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo seizure assay data (Figure 5).

claim: NBI-921352 was effective in preventing seizures at lower brain and plasma concentrations than carbamazepine, phenytoin, and lacosamide.
source: NBI-921352 was effective in preventing seizures at lower brain and plasma concentrations than commonly prescribed sodium channel inhibitor anti-seizure medicines (ASMs) carbamazepine, phenytoin, and lacosamide.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative in vivo efficacy data (Figure 6).

claim: NBI-921352 was well tolerated at higher multiples of the effective plasma and brain concentrations than carbamazepine, phenytoin, and lacosamide.
source: NBI-921352 waswell tolerated at higher multiples of the effective plasma and brain concentrations than those ASMs.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral observation data from in vivo studies (Figure 7).

claim: NBI-921352 is entering phase II proof-of-concept trials for the treatment of SCN8A-developmental epileptic encephalopathy (SCN8A-DEE).
source: NBI-921352 is entering phase II proof-of-concept trials for the treatment of SCN8A-developmental epileptic encephalopathy (SCN8A-DEE) and adult focal-onset seizures.
evidence: This is a statement about the clinical development status of the compound.

claim: NBI-921352 is entering phase II proof-of-concept trials for the treatment of adult focal-onset seizures.
source: NBI-921352 is entering phase II proof-of-concept trials for the treatment of SCN8A-developmental epileptic encephalopathy (SCN8A-DEE) and adult focal-onset seizures.
evidence: This is a statement about the clinical development status of the compound.

claim: NaV1.6 voltage-gated sodium channels are widely expressed in the brain.
source: NaV1.6 voltage-gated sodium channels are widely expressed in the brain and are important contributors to neural excitability (Meisler, 2019; Royeck et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Meisler, 2019; Royeck et al., 2008).

claim: NaV1.6 voltage-gated sodium channels are important contributors to neural excitability.
source: NaV1.6 voltage-gated sodium channels are widely expressed in the brain and are important contributors to neural excitability (Meisler, 2019; Royeck et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Meisler, 2019; Royeck et al., 2008).

claim: Mutations in the SCN8A gene result in malfunction of NaV1.6 sodium channels and cause a spectrum of SCN8A-related syndromes in humans.
source: Mutations in the SCN8A gene result in malfunction of NaV1.6 sodium channels and cause a spectrum of SCN8A-related syndromes in humans, and disruptions of mouse NaV1.6 likewise disrupt normal physiology (Burgess et al., 1995; Gardella and Møller, 2019; Johannesen et al., 2019; Meisler, 2019; Veeramah et al., 2012; Wagnon et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Burgess et al., 1995; Gardella and Møller, 2019; Johannesen et al., 2019; Meisler, 2019; Veeramah et al., 2012; Wagnon et al., 2015).

claim: Disruptions of mouse NaV1.6 disrupt normal physiology.
source: Mutations in the SCN8A gene result in malfunction of NaV1.6 sodium channels and cause a spectrum of SCN8A-related syndromes in humans, and disruptions of mouse NaV1.6 likewise disrupt normal physiology (Burgess et al., 1995; Gardella and Møller, 2019; Johannesen et al., 2019; Meisler, 2019; Veeramah et al., 2012; Wagnon et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Burgess et al., 1995; Gardella and Møller, 2019; Johannesen et al., 2019; Meisler, 2019; Veeramah et al., 2012; Wagnon et al., 2015).

claim: Loss-of-function variants in humans are generally associated with autism spectrum disorders with cognitive and developmental delay without epilepsy.
source: Loss-of-function (LoF) variants in humans are generally associated with autism spectrum disorders with cognitive and developmental delay without epilepsy (Inglis et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2019), but, in some cases, can lead to late-onset seizures.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Inglis et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2019).

claim: Loss-of-function variants in humans can lead to late-onset seizures in some cases.
source: Loss-of-function (LoF) variants in humans are generally associated with autism spectrum disorders with cognitive and developmental delay without epilepsy (Inglis et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2019), but, in some cases, can lead to late-onset seizures.
evidence: This is stated as a general observation in the introduction, though specific citations are not provided for the late-onset seizure claim.

claim: In mice, LoF variants of NaV1.6 lead to motor impairment but increase seizure resistance.
source: In mice, LoF variants of NaV1.6 lead to motor impairment but increase seizure resistance (Hawkins et al., 2011; Martin et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Hawkins et al., 2011; Martin et al., 2007).

claim: Gain-of-function variants in human SCN8A generally result in early-onset SCN8A-related epilepsy syndromes (SCN8A-RES).
source: Gain-of-function (GoF) variants in human SCN8A generally result in early-onset SCN8A-related epilepsy syndromes (SCN8A-RES).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: The most severe of SCN8A-related epilepsy syndromes is SCN8A developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (SCN8A-DEE).
source: The most severe of these epilepsy syndromes is SCN8A developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (SCN8A-DEE) (Gardella and Møller, 2019; Hammer et al., 2016; Johannesen et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Gardella and Møller, 2019; Hammer et al., 2016; Johannesen et al., 2019).

claim: Most SCN8A-RES patients carry de novo heterozygous missense variants that lead to a gain of function of the NaV1.6 channel.
source: Most SCN8A-RES patients carry de novo heterozygous missense variants that lead to a gain of function of the NaV1.6 channel, although inherited and bi-allelic variants have been reported (Gardella and Møller, 2019; Wengert et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Gardella and Møller, 2019; Wengert et al., 2019).

claim: Inherited and bi-allelic variants have been reported in SCN8A-RES.
source: Most SCN8A-RES patients carry de novo heterozygous missense variants that lead to a gain of function of the NaV1.6 channel, although inherited and bi-allelic variants have been reported (Gardella and Møller, 2019; Wengert et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Gardella and Møller, 2019; Wengert et al., 2019).

claim: SCN8A-DEE patients present early in life with seizure onset usually occurring in the first year of life.
source: SCN8A-DEE patients present early in life with seizure onset usually occurring in the first year of life.
evidence: This is stated as established clinical knowledge about SCN8A-DEE.

claim: After seizure onset, SCN8A-DEE patients begin to miss developmental milestones and display additional symptoms, including cognitive and motor delay, hypotonia, and cortical blindness.
source: After seizure onset, patients begin to miss developmental milestones and display additional symptoms, including cognitive and motor delay, hypotonia, and cortical blindness.
evidence: This is stated as established clinical knowledge about SCN8A-DEE.

claim: SCN8A-DEE individuals are predisposed to early death, including sudden unexplained death in epilepsy (SUDEP).
source: SCN8A-DEE individuals are predisposed to early death, including sudden unexplained death in epilepsy (SUDEP).
evidence: This is stated as established clinical knowledge about SCN8A-DEE.

claim: Many SCN8A-RES patients can achieve seizure reduction or seizure freedom upon treatment with anti-seizure medicines (ASMs) that non-selectively inhibit voltage-gated sodium channels, like phenytoin.
source: While SCN8A-RESpatients often have treatment-resistant seizures, many can achieve seizure reduction or seizure freedom upon treatment with anti-seizure medicines (ASMs) that non-selectively inhibit voltage-gated sodium channels, like phenytoin (Boerma et al., 2016; Braakman et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Boerma et al., 2016; Braakman et al., 2017).

claim: SCN8A-RES patients may require doses that are higher than those prescribed for most epilepsy patients and can be more prone to drug-related adverse events.
source: SCN8A-RES patients may require doses that are higher than those prescribed for most epilepsy patients and, as a result, can be more prone to drug-related adverse events (Boerma et al., 2016; Gardella and Møller, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Boerma et al., 2016; Gardella and Møller, 2019).

claim: Many SCN8A patients continue to have uncontrolled seizures as well as extensive comorbidities even with high doses and multiple ASMs.
source: Even with high doses and multiple ASMs, many patients continue to have uncontrolled seizures as well as extensive comorbidities.
evidence: This is stated as established clinical knowledge about SCN8A-RES treatment outcomes.

claim: Existing sodium channel inhibitor ASMs are nonselective, blocking all voltage-gated sodium channel isoforms at similar plasma or brain concentrations.
source: Existing sodium channel inhibitor ASMs are nonselective, blocking all voltage-gated sodium channel isoforms at similar plasma or brain concentrations.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about existing ASMs.

claim: LoF variants of NaV1.1 are known to impair inhibitory interneuron function and cause generalized epilepsy with seizures plus (GEFS+) and SCN1A-DEE (Dravet Syndrome).
source: This lack of selectivity likely limits the benefits of sodium channel inhibitors since LoF variants of NaV1.1 are known toimpair inhibitory interneuron function and causegeneralized epilepsy with seizures plus (GEFS+) and SCN1A-DEE (Dravet Syndrome) (Catterall et al., 2010; Claes et al., 2001; Escayg et al., 2000; Gennaro et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Catterall et al., 2010; Claes et al., 2001; Escayg et al., 2000; Gennaro et al., 2003).

claim: Inhibiting NaV1.1 may counter the benefit of inhibiting the sodium channels of excitatory neurons.
source: Thus, inhibiting NaV1.1 may counter the benefit of inhibiting the sodium channels of excitatory neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known role of NaV1.1 in inhibitory interneurons.

claim: Charge movement in VSD4 has been linked to the voltage dependence of fast inactivation.

claim: Holding the membrane potential at –120 mV induces most channels to reside in the resting state, and brief depolarizations to measure NaV1.6 current enabled the determination of an IC50 of 36 µM (95% CI: 29–47 µM) for rested-state channels.
source: Holding the membrane potential at –120 mV induces most channels to reside in the resting state. Brief depolarizations to measure NaV1.6 current enabled the determination of an IC50of 36 µM (95% CI: 29–47 µM) for rested-state channels.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from voltage-clamp experiments (Figure 3).

claim: Holding the membrane potential at –45 mV encourages channels to transition into inactivated states, and measuring the ability of NBI-921352 to inhibit reopening of activated channels leads to an apparent IC50 of 0.051 µM.
source: Holding the membrane potential at –45 mV encourages channels to transition into inactivated states. Brief hyperpolarizations allow rapid recovery from inactivation for channels that are not bound to drug followed by a short 20ms test pulse to –20 mV to measure currents from unbound channels (see Materials and methods for details). Measuring the ability of NBI-921352 to inhibit reopening of activated channels leads to an apparent IC50 of 0.051 µM (Figures 1 and 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from voltage-clamp experiments (Figures 1 and 3).

claim: NBI-921352 strongly prefers inactivated channels, inhibiting them at concentrations more than 750-fold less than those needed to inhibit rested or 'peak' sodium currents.
source: Thus, NBI-921352 strongly prefers inactivated channels, inhibiting them at concentrations more than 750-fold less than those needed to inhibit rested or 'peak' sodium currents.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the comparison of IC50 values for rested vs. inactivated states.

claim: Elevated persistent and or resurgent currents are believed to underlie or contribute to the pathology of many sodium channel related pathologies.
source: Elevated persistent and or resurgent currents are believed to underlie or contribute to the pathology of many sodium channel related pathologies (Mason et al., 2019; Pan and Cummins, 2020; Potet et al., 2020; Tidball et al., 2020; Zaman et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Mason et al., 2019; Pan and Cummins, 2020; Potet et al., 2020; Tidball et al., 2020; Zaman et al., 2019).

claim: Persistent currents result from channels that are not stably inactivated – a common phenotype for epilepsy-inducing variants in NaV1.6, including N1768D.
source: Persistent currents result from channels that are not stably inactivated – a common phenotype for epilepsy-inducing variants in NaV1.6, including N1768D (Tidball et al., 2020; Wagnon et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Tidball et al., 2020; Wagnon et al., 2015).

claim: NBI-921352 inhibited N1768D NaV1.6 persistent currents with an IC50 of 0.059 µM (95% CI: 0.044–0.082 µM).
source: We found that NBI-921352 inhibited N1768D NaV1.6 persistent currents (measured as the non-inactivating current 10ms after initiation of the depolarizing test pulse) with a similar potency as for activated wild-type NaV1.6 channels with an IC50 of 0.059 µM (95% CI: 0.044–0.082 µM) (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from voltage-clamp experiments (Figure 3).

claim: Resurgent currents occur after repolarizing following a strong depolarization as channels redistribute between closed, open, and inactivated states.
source: Resurgent currents occur after repolarizing following a strong depolarization as channels redistribute between closed, open, and inactivated states (Raman and Bean, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Raman and Bean, 1997).

claim: Resurgent currents are enhanced in many SCN8A-RES variants.
source: These resurgent currents are enhanced in many SCN8A-RES variants (Pan and Cummins, 2020; Raman et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Pan and Cummins, 2020; Raman et al., 1997).

claim: NBI-921352 effectively inhibited resurgent currents from N1768D channels with apparent IC50 of 0.037 µM (95% CI: 0.025–0.060 µM).
source: NBI-921352 also effectively inhibited resurgent currents from N1768D channels with apparent IC50 of 0.037 µM (95% CI: 0.025–0.060 µM).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from voltage-clamp experiments (Figure 3).

claim: Application of 0.250 µM NBI-921352 decreased the maximum firing rate in all three pyramidal neurons tested.
source: Application of 0.250 µM NBI-921352 decreased the maximum firing rate in all three pyramidal neurons tested (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from current-clamp experiments in brain slices (Figure 4A).

claim: Current injection levels > 160 pA led to a significant reduction of the cumulative area under the input output curve (p < 0.05 in a paired two-tailed t-tests) relative to the control condition in pyramidal neurons treated with NBI-921352.
source: Current injection levels > 160 pA led to a significant reduction of the cumulative area under the input output curve (p < 0.05 in a paired two-tailed t-tests) relative to the control condition.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of current-clamp data from pyramidal neurons.

claim: NBI-921352 had no significant effect on the fast-firing inhibitory interneurons tested.
source: In contrast, NBI-921352 had no significant effect on the fast-firing inhibitory interneurons tested (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from current-clamp experiments in brain slices (Figure 4B).

claim: Carbamazepine significantly inhibited action-potential firing in both pyramidal neurons and in fast-spiking interneurons and the degree of inhibition was similar in both types of neurons.
source: Carbamazepine significantly inhibited action-potential firing in both pyramidal neurons and in fast-spiking interneurons and the degree of inhibition was similar in both types of neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from current-clamp experiments in brain slices (Figure 4C and D).

claim: N1768D is a variant of NaV1.6 identified in the first reported SCN8A-DEE patient.
source: N1768D is a variant of NaV1.6 identified in the first reported SCN8A-DEE patient (Veeramah et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Veeramah et al., 2012).

claim: N1768D NaV1.6 channels have impaired voltage-dependent inactivation gating that results in persistent sodium currents and enhanced resurgent currents.
source: N1768D NaV1.6 channels have impaired voltage-dependent inactivation gating that results in persistent sodium currents and enhanced resurgent currents.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the N1768D variant.

claim: Genetically modified mice bearing the N1768D variant (Scn8aN1768D/+) were created and found to be seizure prone, producing a mouse model with a similar phenotype as that observed in SCN8A-DEE patients.
source: Genetically modified mice bearing the same variant (Scn8aN1768D/+) were created and found to be seizure prone, producing a mouse model with a similar phenotype as that observed in SCN8A-DEE patients (Wagnon et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Wagnon et al., 2015).

claim: A mild current stimulation (12 mA) evoked robust generalized tonic-clonic seizures (GTC) with hindlimb extension in Scn8aN1768D/+ mice, but not in wild-type littermates.
source: A mild current stimulation (12 mA) evoked robust generalized tonic-clonic seizures (GTC) with hindlimb extensionin Scn8aN1768D/+ mice, but not in wild-type littermates.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the modified 6 Hz seizure assay.

claim: Oral administration of NBI-921352 2 hr prior to electrical stimulation prevented induction of GTC with hindlimb extension in Scn8aN1768D/+ mice in a dose-dependent manner with an ED50 of 15 mg/kg (95% CI 9.6–23 mg/kg).
source: Oral administration of NBI-921352 2 hr prior to electrical stimulation prevented induction of GTC with hindlimb extension in Scn8aN1768D/+ mice in a dose-dependent manner with a 50% effective dose (ED50) of 15 mg/kg (95% CI 9.6–23 mg/kg, see Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the modified 6 Hz seizure assay in Scn8aN1768D/+ mice (Figure 5A).

claim: The plasma EC50 of NBI-921352 in the Scn8aN1768D/+ mouse model was 0.037 µM (95% CI 0.018–0.090 µM).
source: The plasma 50% effective concentration (EC50) was 0.037 µM (95% CI 0.018–0.090 µM, see Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the modified 6 Hz seizure assay in Scn8aN1768D/+ mice (Figure 5B).

claim: The brain EC50 of NBI-921352 in the Scn8aN1768D/+ mouse model was 0.064 µM (95% CI 0.045–0.091 µM).
source: The brain EC50 was 0.064 µM (95% CI 0.045–0.091 µM, see Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the modified 6 Hz seizure assay in Scn8aN1768D/+ mice (Figure 5C).

claim: The ED50 for NBI-921352 in the wild-type mouse DC-MES assay was 23 mg/kg (95% CI 16–34 mg/kg).
source: The ED50for NBI-921352 was 23 mg/kg (95% CI 16–34 mg/kg, see Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the DC-MES assay in wild-type mice (Figure 5D).

claim: The plasma EC50 of NBI-921352 in the wild-type mouse DC-MES assay was 0.52 µM (95% CI 0.25–1.2 µM).
source: The efficacy of NBI-921352 was also concentration dependent with a plasma EC50 of 0.52 µM (95% CI 0.25–1.2 µM, see Figure 5E) and a brain EC50 of 0.20 µM (95% CI 0.12–0.38 µM, see Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the DC-MES assay in wild-type mice (Figure 5E).

claim: The brain EC50 of NBI-921352 in the wild-type mouse DC-MES assay was 0.20 µM (95% CI 0.12–0.38 µM).
source: The efficacy of NBI-921352 was also concentration dependent with a plasma EC50 of 0.52 µM (95% CI 0.25–1.2 µM, see Figure 5E) and a brain EC50 of 0.20 µM (95% CI 0.12–0.38 µM, see Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the DC-MES assay in wild-type mice (Figure 5F).

claim: The ED50 for NBI-921352 in the wild-type rat DC-MES assay was 3.7 mg/kg (95% CI 2.3–7.6 mg/kg).
source: The ED50 for NBI-921352 was 3.7 mg/kg (95% CI 2.3–7.6 mg/kg, see Figure 5G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the DC-MES assay in wild-type rats (Figure 5G).

claim: The plasma EC50 of NBI-921352 in the wild-type rat DC-MES assay was 0.15 µM (95% CI 0.09–0.31 µM).
source: The efficacy of NBI-921352 was also concentration dependent with a plasma EC50 of 0.15 µM (95% CI 0.09–0.31 µM, see Figure 5H) and a brain EC50 of 0.037 µM (95% CI 0.028–0.054 µM, see Figure 5I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the DC-MES assay in wild-type rats (Figure 5H).

claim: The brain EC50 of NBI-921352 in the wild-type rat DC-MES assay was 0.037 µM (95% CI 0.028–0.054 µM).
source: The efficacy of NBI-921352 was also concentration dependent with a plasma EC50 of 0.15 µM (95% CI 0.09–0.31 µM, see Figure 5H) and a brain EC50 of 0.037 µM (95% CI 0.028–0.054 µM, see Figure 5I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the DC-MES assay in wild-type rats (Figure 5I).

claim: Repeated dosing tended to increase efficacy at lower doses and exposures of NBI-921352 than after a single dose.
source: We found that repeated dosing tended toincrease efficacy at lower doses and exposures of NBI-921352 than after a single dose (Figure 5, red symbols).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from repeated dosing studies (Figure 5, red symbols).

claim: A trend toward improved efficacy was noted in all three assays with repeated dosing, but the improvement was not statistically significant when comparing single-dose groups to repeated-dose groups at the same dose level in the same experiment.
source: A trend toward improved efficacy was noted in all three assays (see red symbols in Figure 5), but the improvement was not statistically significant when comparing single-dose groups to repeated-dose groups at the same dose level in the same experiment.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of repeated dosing data.

claim: NBI-921352 did not appreciably accumulate in the plasma or tissue with repeated dosing.
source: NBI-921352 did not appreciably accumulate in the plasma or tissue and therefore any trends in improved efficacy were not explained by higher drug concentrations.
evidence: This claim is supported by bioanalytical data from repeated dosing studies.

claim: The brain EC50 for carbamazepine in the Scn8aN1768D/+ 6 Hz model was 9.4 µM.
source: The brain EC50s for carbamazepine were 9.4 µM, 44 µM, and 36 µM for the Scn8aN1768D/+ 6 Hz model, WT mouse DC-MES, and WT rat DC-MES models, respectively.

evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo efficacy studies (Figure 6).

source: The brain EC50s for carbamazepine were 9.4 µM, 44 µM, and 36 µM for the Scn8aN1768D/+ 6 Hz model, WT mouse DC-MES, and WT rat DC-MES models, respectively.

source: NBI-921352 was well tolerated in these studies up to a plasma concentration of 71 µM.

claim: Increasing NaV1.6 selectivity can improve the tolerability of NaV inhibitors in rodent-seizure models.
source: This data indicatesthat increasing NaV1.6 selectivity can improve the tolerability of NaV inhibitors in rodent-seizure models.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of BSC/EC50 ratios between NBI-921352 and other ASMs.

claim: Reducing NaV1.1 current is proconvulsant due to the predominance of NaV1.1 in inhibitory interneurons.
source: Reducing NaV1.1 current is proconvulsant due to the predominance of NaV1.1 in inhibitory interneurons (Catterall et al., 2010; Claes et al., 2001; Escayg et al., 2000; Mistry et al., 2014; Yu et al., 2006), while the opposite is true for NaV1.2 and NaV1.6 currents (Ben-Shalom et al., 2017; Hawkins et al., 2011; Martin et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Catterall et al., 2010; Claes et al., 2001; Escayg et al., 2000; Mistry et al., 2014; Yu et al., 2006).

claim: Reducing NaV1.2 and NaV1.6 currents is anticonvulsant.
source: Reducing NaV1.1 current is proconvulsant due to the predominance of NaV1.1 in inhibitory interneurons (Catterall et al., 2010; Claes et al., 2001; Escayg et al., 2000; Mistry et al., 2014; Yu et al., 2006), while the opposite is true for NaV1.2 and NaV1.6 currents (Ben-Shalom et al., 2017; Hawkins et al., 2011; Martin et al., 2007).
evidence: This is implied by the statement that 'the opposite is true for NaV1.2 and NaV1.6 currents' and is supported by citations (Ben-Shalom et al., 2017; Hawkins et al., 2011; Martin et al., 2007).

claim: NaV1.2 and NaV1.6 are more highly expressed in excitatory neurons.
source: NaV1.2 and NaV1.6 are more highly expressed in excitatory neurons (Catterall et al., 2010; Du et al., 2020; Encinas et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Catterall et al., 2010; Du et al., 2020; Encinas et al., 2020).

claim: Lamotrigine has been linked to cardiac liabilities as a consequence of NaV1.5 inhibition.
source: These risks are highlighted by the FDA's recent drug-safety communication for the nonselective NaV inhibitor ASM lamotrigine. Lamotrigine has been linked to cardiac liabilities as a consequence of NaV1.5 inhibition (FDA, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an FDA communication (FDA, 2021).

claim: NBI-921352 represents the first selective inhibitor of NaV1.6 that is suitable for systemic oral administration.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first description of acentrally penetrant, isoform-selective NaV inhibitor for use in CNS indications, including epilepsy. NBI-921352 represents the first selective inhibitor of NaV1.6 that is suitable for systemic oral administration.
evidence: This is stated as a claim about the novelty of the compound.

claim: NBI-921352 did reduce firing in cortical excitatory pyramidal cells.
source: We found that NBI-921352 did reduce firing in cortical excitatory pyramidal cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from current-clamp experiments in brain slices (Figure 4).

claim: Fast-firing inhibitory interneuron firing was not impaired by NBI-921352 and actually showed a trend toward increasing (although not statistically significant).
source: In contrast, fast-firing inhibitory interneuron firing was not impaired and actually showed a trend toward increasing (although not statistically significant).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from current-clamp experiments in brain slices (Figure 4).

claim: NaV1.6 expression has been found in inhibitory interneurons, most well established for Purkinje neurons.
source: The distribution of NaV1.6 to excitatory pyramidal neurons is not absolute, and NaV1.6 expression has also been found in inhibitory interneurons. This is most well established for Purkinje neurons (Raman et al., 1997; Woodruff-Pak et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Raman et al., 1997; Woodruff-Pak et al., 2006).

claim: Deletion of NaV1.6 in Purkinje neurons in mice causes deficits in both cognition and motor control.
source: Deletion of NaV1.6 in Purkinje neurons in mice causes deficits in both cognition and motor control (Levin et al., 2006; Woodruff-Pak et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Levin et al., 2006; Woodruff-Pak et al., 2006).

claim: NaV1.6 is highly expressed at the nodes of Ranvier of both central and peripheral neurons.
source: NaV1.6 is also highly expressed at the nodes of Ranvier of both central and peripheral neurons (Boiko et al., 2001; Caldwell et al., 2000; Herzog et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Boiko et al., 2001; Caldwell et al., 2000; Herzog et al., 2003).

claim: Selective inhibitors of NaV1.6 can cause ataxia and motor symptoms when plasma and brain concentrations are very high.
source: We have found that selective inhibitors of NaV1.6 can cause ataxia and motor symptoms when plasma and brain concentrations are very high (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral observation data from in vivo studies (Figure 7).

claim: Selective inhibition of NaV1.6 provides a robust window between the level of inhibition required to reduce seizure induction and the levels that impair normal behavior.
source: In either case, our data would suggest that selective inhibition of NaV1.6 provides a robust window between the level of inhibition required to reduce seizure induction and the levels that impair normal behavior.
evidence: This is an inference based on the BSC/EC50 ratio data.

claim: R1617Q has been identified in multiple SCN8A-DEE patients.
source: R1617Q has been identified in multiple SCN8A-DEE patients and is in the domain IV voltage-sensor domain (VSD4).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the R1617Q variant.

claim: R1617Q is in the domain IV voltage-sensor domain (VSD4).
source: R1617Q has been identified in multiple SCN8A-DEE patients and is in the domain IV voltage-sensor domain (VSD4).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the location of the R1617Q variant.

claim: NBI-921352 is an aryl sulfonamide with structural similarity to the NaV1.7 targeted aryl sulfonamides where the binding site has been identified as the NaV1.7 VSD4.
source: NBI-921352 is an aryl sulfonamide with structural similarity to the NaV1.7 targeted aryl sulfonamides where the binding site has been identified as the NaV1.7 VSD4 (Ahuja et al., 2015; McCormack et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Ahuja et al., 2015; McCormack et al., 2013) and structural considerations.

claim: The R1617Q variant likely directly or allosterically impairs the tight association of NBI-921252 with NaV1.6 due to its proximity to the binding site.
source: It is likely that the R1617Q directly or allosterically impairs the tight association of NBI-921252 with NaV1.6 due to its proximity to the binding site.
evidence: This is an inference based on the location of the variant and the reduced potency observed.

claim: NBI-921352 remains markedly more potent than existing NaV inhibitor drugs on the R1617Q variant NaV1.6 channel despite the reduction in potency.
source: Despite the reduction in potency, NBI-921352 remains markedly more potent than existing NaV inhibitor drugs on the R1617Q variant NaV1.6 channel.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of NBI-921352 potency to that of existing ASMs.

claim: NBI-921352 may be an effective treatment for SCN8A-DEE patients carrying R1617Q variants, though higher plasma levels of the compound could be required for efficacy in those patients.
source: This would suggest that while NBI-921352 may be an effective treatment for SCN8A-DEE patients carrying R1617Q variants, higher plasma levels of the compound could be required for efficacy in those patients.
evidence: This is speculation based on the reduced potency for the R1617Q variant.

claim: Most known small molecule inhibitors of NaV channels bind preferentially to inactivated gating states of the channels and stabilize the channels in inactivated, non-conductive conformations.
source: Most known small molecule inhibitors of NaV channels, except some marine toxins like tetrodotoxin, bind preferentially to inactivated gating states of the channels and stabilize the channels in inactivated, non-conductive conformations.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about NaV channel inhibitors.

claim: Use-dependent, frequency-dependent, resurgent current-selective, and persistent current-selective inhibition are all consequences of a preference for binding to inactivated channels.
source: Use-dependent, frequency-dependent, resurgent current -selective, and persistent current-selective inhibition are all consequences of a preference for binding to inactivated channels.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about state-dependent inhibition.

claim: Stabilizing inactivated states of the channel reduces persistent and resurgent currents, and this feature has been suggested to contribute to the efficacy of many NaV targeted ASMs including phenytoin, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, lacosamide, cannabidiol, and lamotrigine.
source: Stabilizing inactivated states of the channel reduces persistent and resurgent currents, and this feature has been suggested to contribute to the efficacy of many NaV targeted ASMs including phenytoin, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, lacosamide, cannabidiol, and lamotrigine (Wengert and Patel, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Wengert and Patel, 2021).

claim: NBI-921352 is highly state dependent, with a > 750 fold preference for inactivated channels vs. rested, closed-state channels.
source: NBI-921352 is also highly state dependent, with a > 750 fold preference for inactivated channels vs. rested, closed-state channels (sometimes referred to as peak current).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing IC50 values at different holding potentials (Figure 3).

claim: NBI-921352 binds to the domain IV voltage sensor domain (VSD4), much like GX-936 binds to the chimeric NaV1.7 constructs in Ahuja et al.
source: Based on structural similarities and biophysical behavior, we believe that NBI-921352 binds to the domain IV voltage sensor domain (VSD4), much like GX-936 binds to the chimeric NaV1.7 constructs in Ahuja et al.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural similarities and biophysical behavior, with reference to published work (Ahuja et al.).

claim: The high affinity binding events for NBI-921352 occur only when the VSD4 is in the up state, promoting inactivation.
source: We expect that the high affinity binding events for NBI-921352 occur only when the VSD4 is in the up state, promoting inactivation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the state-dependent behavior of the compound.

claim: NBI-921352 traps channels in the inactivated state and reduces NaV1.6 currents by binding when VSD4 is in the up state.
